title: How to Turn a Partner's Asset Into Your Competitive Weapon
excerptForBlog: Just spoke to Satya and talked about OpenAI needing one the order of 10,000 servers with the latest Nvidia GPUs to beat the best human players at competitive eSports games. This would obviously be a major opportunity for Microsoft to promote Azure relative to other cloud systems. He said he'd talk internally and get back to me soon. Please send me the ideal spec for the individual servers and how they are connected. What ideally do we want Microsoft to do? Sounds like there is a good chance they will do it.

lessonTitle: How to Turn a Partner's Asset Into Your Competitive Weapon
pullQuote: The fastest way to build a moat is to make someone else's resources do the work — before your rivals think to ask.
leadershipTraits: frames deals around the partner's win
honest about what is not yet decided
situation: On June 28, 2017, Elon Musk emailed an OpenAI colleague after a direct call with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. OpenAI needed roughly 10,000 high-end GPU servers — a massive infrastructure cost. Musk had just tested whether Microsoft would supply them. He's writing to figure out exactly what to ask for.
insight:
The hidden move here isn't fundraising. It's **reframing a cost as a marketing asset**. Musk doesn't pitch this as OpenAI needing a favor. He frames it — in his own words — as 'a major opportunity for Microsoft to promote Azure relative to other cloud systems.' He converts OpenAI's resource gap into a competitive weapon for the partner. That's classic platform-strategy thinking: find the player who gains more from your success than you cost them, then make that value obvious.

Notice the sequencing. Musk calls Nadella first, gets a warm signal ('sounds like there is a good chance they will do it'), and only then turns internally to nail down the technical spec. He closed the door before designing the house. That order matters — it avoids wasted internal work and keeps negotiating leverage intact until he knows the ask.
application: Before your next big partnership ask, write one sentence from the partner's perspective: 'This deal helps them because ___.' If you can't fill that blank with something specific to their competitive position — not just 'exposure' or 'learning' — you're not ready to make the call. Lock in directional interest first, then do the detailed scoping work.
